{"id": "43:12/q06", "question": "Why use 'made' for ships and livestock?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:12/q06/p1", "position": "Making fits crafted ships, while created livestock are supplied and trained for people's use.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says ships are manufactured, livestock were already covered by 'created the pairs,' and human thought enables the devising of ships and training of animals. Al-Zajjāj says God created and subjected both sorts of mounts."}]}
{"id": "43:12/q07", "question": "What does min contribute before 'ships'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:12/q07/p1", "position": "It is partitive: some ships and livestock are provided as mounts.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya explicitly calls min partitive."}]}
{"id": "43:12/q08", "question": "What are al-fulk here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:12/q08/p1", "position": "Ships or vessels used at sea.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls them vessels; al-Ṭabarī, al-Māwardī, and al-Qurṭubī say ships. Al-Biqāʿī specifies large seagoing ships. Ibn ʿĀshūr sets them opposite the land-travel camels and cites 36:41–42."}]}
{"id": "43:12/q09", "question": "Why are ships named before livestock?", "turns_on": "Whether sound and display of power, or avoidance of repetition after azwāj, governs the order.", "positions": [{"id": "43:12/q09/p1", "position": "Ships display God's power and wisdom, and the order preserves the ending sound.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī says the explanatory phrase precedes what it explains to preserve the final n-sound; ships come before livestock because they show divine power and wisdom."}, {"id": "43:12/q09/p2", "position": "Ships introduce a fresh gift after the mention of pairs, before livestock return as an anticipated topic.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says pairs already included livestock but not ships, so immediate mention of livestock would repeat. He compares Imru al-Qays's sequence from pleasure-riding a horse to embracing a woman rather than riding a war horse, because the rides differ."}]}
{"id": "43:12/q10", "question": "Which anʿām are meant as mounts?", "turns_on": "Whether anʿām here retains its broad livestock sense, denotes the camels and cattle named in reports, or is restricted by ordinary riding custom to camels; al-Qurṭubī invokes the cow report against cattle.", "positions": [{"id": "43:12/q10/p1", "position": "Camels are the livestock intended for riding here.", "reasons": "Muʿādh, as transmitted by al-Māwardī, and an unnamed view in al-Ṭabrisī specify camels. Al-Qurṭubī holds this and explicitly calls Abū Muʿādh's camel-only view correct: a prophetic report has a ridden cow say it was made for plowing, not riding; the Prophet, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar affirm its speech, though the last two were absent. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says camels alone among livestock are ridden, while horses, mules, and donkeys enter the broader class of mounts. Abū Ḥayyān says custom restricts ridden livestock to camels. Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies the traveled mount as camels and says Arabs call them ships of the land, comparing 36:41–42."}, {"id": "43:12/q10/p2", "position": "Camels and cattle are the livestock named.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Saʿīd b. Jubayr as transmitted by al-Māwardī, al-Ṭabrisī, and al-Qurṭubī give camels and cattle. Al-Qurṭubī argues for camels alone instead: the cow in a prophetic report says it was created for plowing rather than riding."}, {"id": "43:12/q10/p3", "position": "Livestock or beasts of burden generally are among the mounts.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī glosses anʿām as livestock including beasts of burden (3:14) and names camels, horses, mules, and donkeys among land mounts. Al-Biqāʿī calls them livestock used on land. Ibn Kathīr notes their riding and other uses; Study Quran describes cattle as transport and other benefits."}]}
{"id": "43:12/q11", "question": "What is mā and what is understood after 'you ride'?", "turns_on": "Whether mā is a relative requiring an understood object or a verbal noun requiring none.", "positions": [{"id": "43:12/q11/p1", "position": "Mā is a relative pronoun meaning the thing or kind ridden, with an omitted object pronoun.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī gives the relative sense 'that which.' Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn restore mā tarkabūnahu; al-Biqāʿī, al-Ālūsī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr likewise describe the omitted object. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says mā denotes the kind of mount, to which the following pronoun refers. Al-Naḥḥās says the pronoun can be omitted because of the long separation, while masculine or collective feminine agreement could be explicit. Ibn ʿĀshūr says min al-fulk wa-l-anʿām explains the relative mā and calls deletion of its connected accusative pronoun common. Al-Ālūsī cites 29:65 and 16:8 in explaining the ship/mount constructions."}, {"id": "43:12/q11/p2", "position": "Mā can be a verbal noun, so no omitted pronoun is needed.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās gives this as an alternative to the relative analysis."}]}
{"id": "43:12/q12", "question": "How does one verb for riding apply to animals and ships?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:12/q12/p1", "position": "The direct construction used for animals is extended to ships and predominates over the ship construction with fī.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Samīn, al-Biqāʿī, al-Ālūsī, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr contrast direct animal-riding with riding in ships; most cite the direct pattern's strength. Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī cite 29:65 for ships and 16:8 for animals. Al-Bayḍāwī adds possible preference for animals made for riding or common over rare usage. Al-Bursawī describes the same sea/land contrast. Abū Ḥayyān says rakiba can directly take an object where another construction takes fī, although he calls the verb intransitive with respect to its complement here. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the object is clear, so direct transitivity generalizes and the relative object pronoun is omitted; literally one mounts an animal, while ship boarding is a figurative extension through likeness of motion (11:41)."}]}
{"id": "43:12/q13", "question": "How does agreement with mā explain the following verse's 'backs' and pronouns?", "turns_on": "Whether form, collective sense, alternation between them, or nontrue feminine gender accounts for the agreement.", "positions": [{"id": "43:12/q13/p1", "position": "Masculine agreement follows the grammatical form of the relative mā.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda, as transmitted by al-Rāzī, explains the masculine by the understood 'what you ride'; al-Majāz likewise says the masculine follows mā. Abū Ḥayyān objects to using mā tarkabūn as a simple parallel, since agreement can shift from form to sense and back in the following verse."}, {"id": "43:12/q13/p2", "position": "Plural 'backs' follows the collective sense of singular mā.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, reported by al-Thaʿlabī and al-Rāzī, compares singular collectives such as army, host, and cavalry. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the pronoun can refer to the kind of mount expressed by mā."}, {"id": "43:12/q13/p3", "position": "Agreement can move from mā's form to its collective sense and back to singular form.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says the next verse can use plural 'backs' according to sense and then a singular pronoun according to form; he rejects mā tarkabūn as an opposing parallel (43:13)."}, {"id": "43:12/q13/p4", "position": "The feminine gender here is not true grammatical gender, allowing forms to vary.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports this third explanation and compares a phrase about one among women who agrees with you."}]}
{"id": "43:12/q14", "question": "What benefits and lesson do the provided mounts convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:12/q14/p1", "position": "God supplies and makes sea and land transport usable for people's travel and livelihood as a divine blessing.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī names sea travel and livelihood and travel by camels, horses, mules, and donkeys to destinations. Al-Māwardī, al-Baghawī, al-Rāzī, and al-Biqāʿī contrast land and sea journeys; al-Biqāʿī calls both gifts. Al-Zajjāj says God created and subjected both. Ibn Kathīr adds eating animal meat and drinking milk. Study Quran calls seafaring and cattle blessings, adding loads, warmth/clothing, food/drink, and beauty as signs of beneficence, with 14:32, 17:66, 22:65, 30:46, 6:142, 16:5, 16:66, 16:79, 23:21–22, 36:72, and 40:79. Kuranyolu says riding, load-carrying, guarding, plowing, and threshing depend on domestication; without it those services fail. Study Quran says subjection of creation reveals dependence on Divine Aid (31:20)."}]}
{"id": "43:12/q15", "question": "What does iqran in the rider's response mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:12/q15/p1", "position": "It means having the ability or capacity to manage the mount.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī illustrates it with saying one can handle a camel when able to manage it."}]}
{"id": "43:12/q16", "question": "What travel remembrance or instruction is associated with these mounts?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:12/q16/p1", "position": "Riders should invoke God's name and recognize that God carries and enables them.", "reasons": "Abū Lās al-Khuzāʿī reports the Prophet saying every camel has a devil on its hump: riders should name God, tame the camel for their needs, and remember God carries them. Ibn Kathīr gives a parallel report with a devil on every camel's back and the instruction to say God's name and then pursue one's needs without restraint; he identifies Abū Lās as Muḥammad b. al-Aswad b. Khalaf. Study Quran says the supplication is commonly used on land journeys, while 11:41 is advised for sea journeys, and cites 28:85. Its account of human dependence on Divine Aid cites 31:20."}]}
{"id": "43:12/q17", "question": "How does this verse's sequence connect to its context?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:12/q17/p1", "position": "The divine acts are blessings and proof against polytheism, moving from life's supports to livelihood and travel.", "reasons": "Ib

n ʿAṭiyya calls these acts blessings for humanity and proof against every disbelieving polytheist. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the passage shifts from supports of life to production and trade travel and repeats the relative noun. Al-Biqāʿī says the widened notion of pairs includes contrasting transport, sea ships and land livestock."}]}
{"id": "43:12/q18", "question": "Do the second-person pronouns in this passage constitute a rhetorical shift?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:12/q18/p1", "position": "No; the eleven second-person pronouns across the four verses continue the expected address.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says they are not iltifāt."}]}
{"id": "43:12/q19", "question": "How does the sūrah's larger theme frame this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:12/q19/p1", "position": "It belongs to a unified challenge to the Makkan idolaters' worldview and objections.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says every part of Sūrah al-Zukhruf relates deeply to its central theme and the whole sūrah is harmonious. Study Quran says the sūrah answers Makkan idolaters' objections and addresses forms of disbelief."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q01", "question": "What does istawā mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether istiwāʾ describes taking one's place on the vehicle or mastery over it.", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q01/p1", "position": "To settle, sit, or mount a conveyance.", "reasons": "Muqātil glosses it as sitting; al-Māwardī as riding, al-Dāmghānī as riding or boarding. Al-Biqāʿī adds upright balance, steadiness, security and ease. Ibn ʿĀshūr says climbing aboard; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says settling on it."}, {"id": "43:13/q01/p2", "position": "To gain mastery over the conveyance.", "reasons": "Asad cites al-Jawharī, al-Rāghib, Lisān al-ʿArab, and Lane for the connotation of mastery."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q02", "question": "What is the force of the lām in litastawū?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause gives God's end, the ensuing result, or a second-person imperative; the rarity of the last construction is disputed.", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q02/p1", "position": "It is a lām of purpose: conveyances were made so people might ride.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān calls this most natural; al-Samīn calls it apparent and attaches it to jaʿala; al-Ālūsī prefers it and reports Abū Ḥayyān's account of the majority view. Ibn ʿAṭiyya allows it."}, {"id": "43:13/q02/p2", "position": "It may be a lām of consequence or result.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥūfī allows this category; al-Samīn also allows it and attaches it to jaʿala; al-Ālūsī reports the allowance."}, {"id": "43:13/q02/p3", "position": "It may be a command lām: 'let you mount.'", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya allows this; al-Zajjāj regards the second-person form as good Arabic. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn call it far-fetched because lām imperatives rarely take second-person tāʾ. The anomalous 10:58 reading, a poem with لتقم, and a Prophetic phrase are cited; the Prophetic wording may have been transmitted by meaning. Al-Ālūsī repeats those examples."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q03", "question": "What conveyances are meant by the backs?", "turns_on": "Whether 'backs' extends naturally to ships' upper surfaces or primarily names animal backs.", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q03/p1", "position": "The backs or upper surfaces of what people ride, including animals and ships.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, and Asad explicitly include both. Ibn ʿĀshūr says ship decks or interiors can be spoken of by the shared sense of backs and upper surfaces, citing 23:28; large ships shelter riders. Al-Ālūsī says 'settling' especially suits animals while wording covers all."}, {"id": "43:13/q03/p2", "position": "Animal mounts, especially camels, are in view.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies male and female camels. Mujāhid lists camels, horses, mules and donkeys. Al-Qurṭubī argues ships are boarded by their undersides, though he allows their submerged outside to count as inside; Bursawī says backs literally suit livestock, which gives them semantic priority."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q04", "question": "Why are 'backs' plural while its pronoun is singular masculine?", "turns_on": "Whether agreement is explained through relative mā, a generic singular, or the collective noun al-fulk.", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q04/p1", "position": "The pronoun follows singular masculine mā, while plural 'backs' follows its collective meaning.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda, al-Naḥḥās, al-Baghawī and others trace the pronoun to mā; al-Farrāʾ compares collective army or troop. The Basran grammarian says mā tarkabūn is masculine and notes anʿām can take either gender (16:66, 16:69). Al-Biqāʿī adds that ʿalayhi follows form and masculine wording may signal strength. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the pronoun covers ships and livestock."}, {"id": "43:13/q04/p2", "position": "The singular pronoun may follow the generic singular noun or collective ship noun.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ compares 'the dirham became numerous'; another grammarian says al-fulk is collective, permitting plural backs with a singular pronoun and singular or plural actions."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q05", "question": "Which blessing should a rider recall?", "turns_on": "Whether the blessing is the immediate transport, Islam, or divine gifts more broadly.", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q05/p1", "position": "God's subjection and provision of the conveyance for land or sea travel.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies the mount and praise; al-Kalbī says thank God for carrying the rider; Ibn ʿAbbās calls conveyances an honor to Adam's children, citing 17:70. Al-Rāzī includes sea, wind and ship, which humans did not devise by themselves. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī includes transport of loads (14:32, 16:7); Study Quran catalogs other cattle uses and signs."}, {"id": "43:13/q05/p2", "position": "The blessing especially includes Islam, Muhammad, and belonging to the best community.", "reasons": "Shahr names Islam; the reports of Abū Mijlaz and the Prophet's family prescribe thanks for Islam, Muhammad, and the community before the riding formula. The names differ between al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn in the transmitted reports."}, {"id": "43:13/q05/p3", "position": "The words may recall God's blessings generally, beyond this ride.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī offers this move from the vehicle to God Himself; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says praise can concern blessing in every circumstance."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q06", "question": "How is the blessing to be remembered and thanked?", "turns_on": "Whether 'remember' requires verbal thanks as well as inward acknowledgment, and whether the following tasbīḥ is itself that thanks.", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q06/p1", "position": "Recognize the blessing inwardly and express gratitude aloud.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī distinguish heart awareness from spoken glorification. Al-Ḥasan's correction of a rider who only glorified God illustrates explicit praise. Al-Biqāʿī adds gratitude of limbs. Bursawī says heart remembrance explains the verb choice and cites the report that God looks to hearts and intentions. Ibn ʿĀshūr says riding's experienced benefit makes recollection timely and effective, while the wording counters polytheists thanking other gods; he compares taught praise and supplication at 1:2 and 2:286. Al-Ālūsī finds the joint inward and verbal account sound. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī transmits al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī asking a man who said the riding glorification whether he had been commanded to say it."}, {"id": "43:13/q06/p2", "position": "Inward recognition can suffice for the remembrance before glorification.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says a rider may begin with glorification if the blessing of the mount and other blessings are recognized inwardly."}, {"id": "43:13/q06/p3", "position": "Remembering means saying praise for the mount.", "reasons": "Muqātil states the spoken phrase 'Praise be to God'; al-Ṭabrisī combines remembering, thanking, and declaring God unlike creatures."}, {"id": "43:13/q06/p4", "position": "Gratitude for the blessing is distinct from the ensuing glorification.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says remembering a blessing in use normally means thanking its giver; the subsequent tasbīḥ has another function, and variant reports include both praise and glorification."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q07", "question": "Why does thumma place remembrance after mounting?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q07/p1", "position": "Remembrance is a higher aim after the transport benefit, and should arise when the benefit is felt.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī sees delay as marking a lofty goal and the Lord's nurturing kindness. Ibn ʿĀshūr says gratitude while experiencing the ride is more affecting and less apt to lapse; al-Biqāʿī calls familiar stability extraordinary beside unrideable animals and uncaring sea objects."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q08", "question": "How does the 'when' clause time the commanded remembrance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q08/p1", "position": "A command with 'when' can be performed before, at, or after the condition, depending on its action.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī illustrates the possibilities with washing before prayer, measured recitation at its occasion, and hunting or Friday prayer after their conditions."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q09", "question": "What riding invocation is reported from ʿAlī and the Prophet?", "turns_on": "The transmitted practices differ by reporter, sequence, added phrases, and grading.", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q09/p1", "position": "At the stirrup invoke God's name; once mounted, praise Him, recite the verse, magnify Him, and seek forgiveness.", "reasons": "ʿAlī says the Prophet acted likewise. Reports vary in whether they specify three repetitions of praise, takbīr, tasbīḥ or tahlīl. The Prophet marvels that the penitent knows only God forgives. Al-Tirmidhī's grading is cited as ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ; al-Ālūsī calls it authentic. Ibn Ḥibbān says the expanded words permit adding phrases. Al-Qurṭubī names Abū Dāwūd al-Ṭayālisī and Ibn Khuwayzimindād as transmitters; al-Thaʿlabī gives no gr

ading."}, {"id": "43:13/q09/p2", "position": "ʿAlqama invoked God's name before mounting, praised Him once seated, and recited the formula when the animal rose.", "reasons": "Ibrāhīm transmits ʿAlqama ibn Qays's practice."}, {"id": "43:13/q09/p3", "position": "Ṭāwūs or his father acknowledged the ride as God's bounty, praised Him, then recited the verse.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Razzāq attributes the practice to Ṭāwūs's father; al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and al-Durr report Ṭāwūs himself. The wordings name favor, grace, or gift."}, {"id": "43:13/q09/p4", "position": "The Prophet recited the riding formula and then prayed for a pious, easy and protected journey and a thankful return.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmar's reports add three opening takbīrs, righteousness, accepted deeds, divine company and care for family; on return he says they come back repentant, worshipping and praising God. Al-Tirmidhī grades one route ḥasan gharīb. Ibn Kathīr lists Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, Nasāʾī, Tirmidhī through Abū al-Zubayr; Ibn Ḥibbān adduces another transmission against the claim Ḥammād b. Salama alone carried that report. Abū Dāwūd adds the troops' takbīr uphill and tasbīḥ downhill."}, {"id": "43:13/q09/p5", "position": "The Prophet magnified, praised, glorified and declared God one, then reclined and laughed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reports that God smiles toward a Muslim rider who does likewise. Aḥmad alone transmits it according to Ibn Kathīr. The reports vary over the threefold phrases and mention a single tahlīl."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q10", "question": "What should be said on boarding a ship or disembarking?", "turns_on": "Whether the present formula covers ships or the separate scriptural boarding formula governs sea travel.", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q10/p1", "position": "On ships say 11:41, 'In God's name is its course and anchorage'; on disembarking ask for a blessed landing (23:29).", "reasons": "Qatāda and several commentators distinguish this from the animal mounting formula. Al-Rāzī sets beside them a prayer for entering a dwelling. One report has al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī recite 11:41 and 39:67 aboard. Study Quran describes the land and sea practice."}, {"id": "43:13/q10/p2", "position": "The remembrance and glorification in this passage apply to ships as well as animals.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Ālūsī extend the formula to sea travel; al-Thaʿlabī's report has Qatāda teach words for both ships and livestock."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q11", "question": "What happens in reports when riders omit the remembrance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q11/p1", "position": "Satan urges an unremembering rider to sing or waste time in fantasies.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes this to the Prophet; al-Qurṭubī reports Mujāhid's version and says al-Naḥḥās transmitted it."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q12", "question": "What do reports say about a devil on a camel?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q12/p1", "position": "A devil is on each camel's hump; invoke God and ride or tame it humbly, since God carries the rider.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī also transmits Abū Jaʿfar's account through ʿAmr ibn Dīnār. Al-Durr preserves versions from Muḥammad b. Ḥamza, Abū Hurayra and Abū Lās. Al-Ālūsī says Aḥmad and others transmit a version."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q13", "question": "What happened to the rider who boasted he could master his camel?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q13/p1", "position": "The camel bucked or ran, threw the boasting rider, and broke his neck.", "reasons": "Sulaymān ibn Yasār's versions describe an emaciated, still or stubborn camel, while Ibn al-ʿArabī calls the rider a Bedouin; al-Ālūsī has a powerful camel. These details vary across the transmission. Al-Qurṭubī explains al-jawr baʿd al-kawr in the added travel prayer as affairs scattering after they were ordered."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q14", "question": "What conduct does this riding remembrance require?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q14/p1", "position": "Recall the formula when mounting, especially for travel, while spoken recitation is not obligatory.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī recommends adding prayers for divine company, safety from travel hardship and bad return; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls praise for Islam, Muhammad, or all circumstances the rider's sunnah. Ibn Ḥibbān permits adding phrases to the supplication."}, {"id": "43:13/q14/p2", "position": "Riding should be for need, God's path, or a licit purpose, without heedless indulgence.", "reasons": "Abū Bakr b. Ṭāhir excludes amusement and pride. Al-Qurṭubī censures wine and instruments on pleasure trips, citing al-Zamakhsharī's story of a ruler drunk through a month's ride, and contrasts this with commanded remembrance. Elmalılı says journeying should recall return to God."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q15", "question": "May someone ritually impure say the riding words?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q15/p1", "position": "Yes, if the intention is supplication rather than Qur'anic recitation.", "reasons": "Al-Nawawī gives the travel words among examples of Qur'anic phrases used with another intention."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q16", "question": "Is the verse's instruction to say the formula a statement or a command?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q16/p1", "position": "Its declarative form carries an instruction to say the words.", "reasons": "The author of al-Naẓm reasons that if it were mere report, all people would actually do it; 51:56 similarly means they were created to be commanded to worship. Al-Ālūsī says the utterance's declarative wording implies a request."}]}
{"id": "43:13/q17", "question": "What does subḥāna express in the formula?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q17/p1", "position": "It exalts God above defect and partners, with wonder at His power to subject the vehicle.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī rejects polytheists' partners and descriptions; al-Ṭabrisī says God is unlike created things. Ibn ʿĀshūr says tasbīḥ explicitly negates defects and implicitly affirms perfections, gathering praise. Bursawī locates wonder in the mount's subjection. {"id": "43:13/q21", "question": "What does muqrinīn mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the lexical emphasis is ability to match and control, companionship or coupling, ownership, or an attested contrary usage.", "positions": [{"id": "43:13/q21/p1", "position": "Able or strong enough to master, control, or match the conveyance.", "reasons": "Al-Kumayt, Ibn Hurmā and ʿAmr b. {"id": "43:14/q01", "question": "What return to the Lord does the declaration describe?", "turns_on": "Whether the return is the final resurrection, an act of prayer, safe homecoming, or an inward return; the Study Quran explicitly offers prayer and the Hereafter as alternatives.", "positions": [{"id": "43:14/q01/p1", "position": "People return to God after death, for resurrection and the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj and al-Tabataba'i call it an affirmation of resurrection; al-Tha'labi, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Ashur specify resurrection, while Ibn Ashur adds reckoning and recompense. {"id": "43:14/q04", "question": "Why is return to God recalled while riding?", "turns_on": "The notes variously connect riding with sudden death, the analogy between journeys, the bier, continuing divine favor, and safe homecoming; al-Baydawi and al-Biqa'i explicitly mark alternatives.", "positions": [{"id": "43:14/q04/p1", "position": "Travel's danger can bring sudden death, so riders should remember their certain meeting with God.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari names falls, runaway animals and shipwreck; al-Razi links ships and animals to possible death; al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Bursevi add drowning, stumbling and fatal accidents, urging readiness through reform, remembrance and speech. {"id": "43:23/q01", "question": "How does 'likewise' connect these earlier peoples to Quraysh?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:23/q01/p1", "position": "Earlier peoples answered their warners with the same appeal to ancestral religion as Quraysh, a recurring rejection that consoles Muhammad and exposes inherited imitation as an old error.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj, al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir, and al-Tabataba'i compare earlier deniers with the Meccans; al-Tabari also cites 34:34.
